Medical Certificates (FAR 61.23) & Basic Med 						AI.III.A.K3
Medical Certificates
What is it?
A routine medical exam from an FAA authorized Aviation Medical Examiner (AME)
3 different classes – 1st, 2nd, 3rd class
Who Needs it? (More details / requirements in FAR 61.23)
1st Class: Generally required when exercising PIC privileges of an ATP
2nd Class: Generally required when SIC at an airline or to use your commercial pilot certificate
3rd Class: Required when
Exercising the privileges of a Private, Recreational, or Student Pilot certificate
Exercising the privileges of a CFI certificate as PIC or required crewmember
Taking a practical test
Performing duties as an Examiner
FAR 61.23(b) – A medical is not required when:
Exercising privilege of a CFI certificate if not acting as PIC / serving as a required crewmember
Exercising the privileges of a ground instructor certificate
A military pilot can show evidence of an up-to-date medical examination
The flight cannot require higher than a 3rd class medical and must be in US airspace
Class & Duration (FAR 61.23(d))
First Class
Under 40 on the date of the exam - Expires at the end of the last day of the:
12th month for 1st class activities
12th month for 2nd class activities
60th month for 3rd class activities (under 40 years old)
40 or older on the date of the exam - Expires at the end of the last day of the:
6th month for 1st class activities
12th month for 2nd class activities
24th month for 3rd class activities (over 40 years old)
Second Class
Under 40 on the date of the exam - Expires at the end of the last day of the:
12th month for 2nd class activities
60th month for 3rd class activities
40 or older on the date of the exam - Expires at the end of the last day of the:
12th month for 2nd class activities
24th month for 3rd class activities
Third Class
Under 40 on the date of the exam - Expires at the end of the last day of the:
60th month
40 or older on the date of the exam - Expires at the end of the last day of the:
24th month
How to find an AME - FAA.gov AME Locator
FAA Directory of AMEs can be found at FSDOs, FSSs, FAA Offices
Once you have a medical, how is it regulated?
FAR 61.53 (Prohibition on operations during medical deficiency) prohibits flying if you:
Know of any medical condition that would prevent you from obtaining a medical
Are taking medication/receiving treatment that would prevent you from obtaining a medical
Once obtained, it is self-regulating (be safe, and conservative)
Medical Certificate with a Possible Medical Deficiency
Even with a medical deficiency, a medical certificate may be able to be issued
15 disqualifying medical conditions (listed here)
Special Issuance Authorization is required (FAR 67.401)
With few exceptions, all disqualifying conditions may be considered for special issuance
BasicMed & Using a Driver’s License – FAR 61.23(c)
A way to fly without a holding a medical certificate
FAA BasicMed Info; FAA BasicMed FAQ
Applicable when operating under FAR 61.113(i), and exercising the privileges of:
A learner, recreational or private pilot certificate
A flight instructor certificate and acting as PIC or a required crewmember
A person using their driver’s license must:
Comply with all medical requirements associated with the license
Have held a medical certificate after July 14, 2006
Have completed the medical education course in the last 24 months
Have received a medical exam in the past 48 months using the directed exam checklist
Have not had the most recently held medical certificate revoked, suspended, or withdrawn
Be under the care of a physician if diagnosed with a condition that may affect flight abilities
FAR 61.113(i) requires (updated to reflect Nov 12, 2024 changes):
Aircraft: Authorized for no more than 7 occupants, Max takeoff weight ≤ 12,500 lbs.
Flight: In the US, less than 18,000’ and 250 knots, not for compensation/hire
Pilot: Has medical exam checklist and certificate of course completion in logbook
Passengers: 6

Required Logbook Entries (FAR 61.51 & 61.189)
61.189: A flight instructor must sign the logbook of each person they have given flight or ground training
61.51: Must document training/experience to meet the requirements for a certificate, rating, or review
Logbook must show:
Date, Total flight/lesson time; location of departure/arrival (location for a simulator); type and identification of aircraft/simulator/training device; name of the safety pilot (if used)

Privileges & Limitations 									AI.III.A.K2
Sport Pilot - FAR 61. 89(c) & 61.315 (61.316 to be added effective October 22, 2025)
New MOSAIC (Modernization of Special Airworthiness Certification) Overview
Effective October 22, 2025 – Sport Pilots may fly aircraft with:
Max Seating: Up to 4 seats (still limited to 2 occupants – pilot + 1 passenger)
Max Takeoff Weight: None (was 1,320 lbs.)
Max Stall Speed: 59 KCAS – clean configuration (up from 45 KCAS)
Max Airspeed: None (but light-sport category aircraft will be limited to 250 KCAS)
Prop &  Gear: Retractable landing gear and manual controllable-pitch props (with training & endorsements)
Night operation (with training & endorsements and a 3rd class medical or BasicMed)
Driver’s License in lieu of an FAA medical or BasicMed (only for day VFR ops)
Private Pilots or higher can exercise Sport Pilot privileges under their existing certificate beginning October 22, 2025, without any additional paperwork or checkrides
Light-Sport Aircraft (LSA) definition is removed from regs, Light-Sport Category is implemented
LSA definition is removed from FAR 1.1 and new aircraft design and performance requirements for airworthiness certification in the light-sport category are relocated to 22.100

Aircraft eligible for Light-Sport certification now defined by performance (stall speed, etc.) not weight – allowing up to 4 seats, retractable gear, constant-speed props, electric/hybrid propulsion, composite construction, etc.
Performance envelope broadened: up to 61 KCAS stall speed in landing configuration, speeds up to 250 knots allowed
Light-Sport Category Aircraft
Max Weight: None (was 1,320 lbs.)
Max Stall Speed: 61 KCAS (flaps extended)
Max Airspeed: 250 KCAS
Engines: Number & type of engine limitation is removed
Gear: Fixed or retractable
Prop: Any
Design & Approval: Under Part 22 Standards
Expanded Aircraft Types: Helicopters, power-lift, gyroplanes, eVTOLs

Pilot Currency (FAR 61.57) 									AI.III.A.K1
Pilot in Command
FAR 61.57(a) – To carry passengers: 3 takeoffs and landings in the last 90 days
Sole manipulator of the flight controls in the same category, class, type aircraft
Tailwheel landings must be to a full stop
FAR 61.57(b) – To carry passengers 1 hour after sunset to 1 hour before sunrise:
3 takeoffs and landings in the last 90 days to a full stop (1 hour after to 1 hour before)
Sole manipulator of the flight controls in the same category, class, type aircraft
FAR 61.57(c) & (d) - To act as PIC under IFR within the preceding 6 months:
6 instrument approaches, holding procedures, and intercepting/tracking courses
If the pilot has failed to meet the experience requirements (above) for more than 6 calendar months, currency may only be reestablished through an instrument proficiency check (IPC)
Flight Reviews (FAR 61.56)
To act as PIC, a flight review/logbook endorsement are required within the last 24 months
FAR 61.56(d) – Not necessary if any of the following have been passed (last 24 months):
Proficiency check or practical test for a pilot certificate, rating, or operating privilege
A practical test for a flight instructor certificate, an additional rating on a flight instructor certificate, renewal, or reinstatement of a flight instructor certificate
Not required if one or more phases of a pilot proficiency award program has been completed
A Student Pilot in training, with a current solo flight endorsement does not need a flight review
RM: Proficiency versus Currency 								AI.III.A.R1
Currency is the minimum required by law to legally fly
Proficiency is a level of understanding and ability that creates a safe and competent pilot
Just because you are current does not mean you are proficient
RM: Flying Unfamiliar Aircraft 								AI.III.A.R2
Ensure proficiency – Just because you can, doesn’t mean you’re proficient or safe
Required Documents 										AI.III.A.K4
FAR 61.3: Requirement for Certificates, Ratings, and Authorizations
Pilot Certificate (& Flight Instructor Certificate, if exercising privileges)
Government Issued Photo Identification
Medical Certificate
FAR 61.51(i) Presentation of Documents
Must present pilot certificate, medical, logbook, or any other record required by part 61 on request
Student Pilot on solo cross-country flights must carry:
Pilot logbook with endorsements, Student Pilot certificate, any other certificate required by Part 61
Sport pilot must carry their logbook or other evidence of required instructor endorsements on all flights
Recreational pilot must carry their logbook with required instructor endorsements on all solo flights:
> 50 nm from the airport at which the training was received
Within airspace requiring communication with ATC
Conducted between sunset & sunrise, or
In an aircraft for which the pilot doesn’t hold an appropriate category or class rating
Instructor with a sport pilot rating must carry:
Logbook or other evidence of required instructor endorsements when providing flight training
Conclusion: Brief review of the main point

Airworthiness 											AI.III.B.K1
Basically, we’re verifying that the aircraft is safe to fly and meets all required regulations
Key Conditions for Airworthiness – The aircraft:
Conforms to its type certificate (matches FAA approved specifications)
Is in a condition for safe flight (no defects or issues that could compromise safety)

paragraphs.text: III.C. Weather Information
Introduction
How
Atmospheric Composition & Stability 							AI.III.C.K3a
4 gases make up 99.998% of the atmosphere
Nitrogen, Oxygen, Argon, and Carbon Dioxide
The Atmosphere is divided into 5 concentric layers
Troposphere
Surface up to about 36,000’ high (varies with temperature variations)
Temperature decreases with height & almost all weather occurs in this region
Transition layer between the troposphere and they layer above is called the tropopause
Stratosphere
Tropopause up to 31 miles high (Holds 19% of the atmosphere’s gases, but little water)
Temperature increases with height due to the absorption of UV radiation
Commercial aircraft often cruise in the lower stratosphere to avoid turbulence/convection
Mesosphere
Stratopause to about 53 miles above the Earth.
Gases continue to thin leading to a decrease in temperature with height
Thermosphere
Mesopause to 430 miles above the Earth (known as the upper atmosphere)
Temp increases with height and can reach 2,000 degrees Celsius near the top of the layer
High energy UV and X-ray radiation from the sun is absorbed
Exosphere
Thermopause to 6,200 miles above the surface (outermost layer of the atmosphere)
Atoms and molecules escape into space, and where satellites orbit the Earth
Standard Atmosphere
Average of conditions throughout the atmosphere for all latitudes, seasons, and altitudes
Wind 												AI.III.C.K3b
Air in motion relative to the surface. Wind causes the formation, dissipation, and redistribution of weather
Forces that Affect the Wind
Pressure Gradient Force (PGF)
Wind flows from areas of high to low pressure. These different pressures create the PGF
When a pressure difference develops, the PGF makes the wind blow to equalize the differences
Wind speed is proportional to PGF which is proportional to the contour/isobar gradient
Coriolis Force (pictured, right)
Deflects air to the right in the Northern Hemisphere & left in the Southern Hemisphere
At a right angle to wind direction
Directly proportional to wind speed
If wind speed doubles, Coriolis doubles
Coriolis varies with latitude
Zero at the equator & maximum at each pole
Friction
Friction between wind and the surface slows the wind
Rougher terrain and stronger winds = greater friction
Insignificant above the lowest few thousand feet or so
Above the friction layer, only the PGF and Coriolis force affect the horizontal motion of the air
Adverse Winds
Wind Shear
What is it?
A sudden, drastic change in wind speed and/or direction over a very small area
Can occur at any altitude
Low-level wind shear is especially hazardous due to the proximity to the ground
Low-level wind shear is commonly associated with passing frontal systems, thunderstorms, temperature inversions, and strong upper-level winds (> 25 knots)
Why is it dangerous?
Can cause violent updrafts/downdrafts, and abrupt changes to horizontal movement
It can rapidly change performance and disrupt the normal flight attitude, for example:
A tailwind can quickly change to a headwind, increasing airspeed and performance
A headwind can quickly change to a tailwind, decreasing airspeed and performance
Although reported, it often remains undetected
Be alert for wind shear, especially when flying around thunderstorms & frontal systems
Mountain Waves (AIM 7-6-7j)
What is it?
The atmosphere is a fluid in motion
Just as a stream develops waves & eddies as it passes obstructions, so does the atmosphere
When the atmosphere encounters a mountainous barrier, and the wind is sufficiently strong and the atmosphere is stable, a wave will develop
Air hits the upwind side, creating a smooth updraft
Passing the crest, it becomes a turbulent downdraft
Turns into a wave that can last for miles
Hazards
Strong down drafts and/or turbulence on the immediate leeward side of the mountain
Visual Indicators
Sharp-edged, lens-shaped lenticular clouds
With sufficient moisture, clouds can include:
Cap clouds, Cirrocumulus Standing Lenticular (CCSL), Altocumulus Standing Lenticular (ACSL), and rotor clouds
These clouds provide evidence of mountain waves, but may be absent if the air is too dry
Types of Waves
For significantly more info, Aviation Weather Handbook Ch. 16 discusses many wave types
Gravity Waves, Kelvin-Helmholtz (K-H) Waves, Vertically Propagating Mountain Waves, Trapped Lee Waves, and more
Temperature											AI.III.C.K3c
Represents the average kinetic energy of the molecules in matte
Heat Transfer
Heat transfer is a transfer of energy due to temperature difference
The heat source for the planet is the sun. Energy from the sun is transferred to the Earth’s surface. There are 3 ways heat is transferred into and through our atmosphere:
Radiation: Ex. Being near a fireplace, the sun radiating heat to the earth
Conduction: Transfer of energy from one substance to another
Convection: Transport of heat within a fluid, such as air or water
Because air is a poor thermal conductor, convection plays a vital role in the Earth’s atmospheric heat transfer process
Temperature & the Earth/Atmosphere
Thermal Response: Water is much more resistant to temperature changes than land
Temperature Variations with Altitude
Temperature generally decreases at an average of 2o Celsius per 1,000’
But in the troposphere, temperature can remain constant or increase with altitude changes
Isothermal Layer: An atmospheric layer where temperature remains constant with height
Temperature Inversion: A layer in which the temperature increases with altitude
Moisture & Precipitation 									AI.III.C.K3d
Ingredients for Precipitation
Water Vapor
Sufficient Lifting - condenses the water vapor into clouds
Growth Process - allows cold droplets to grow large and heavy enough to fall as precipitation
Two growth processes allow cloud droplets to grow large enough to fall as precipitation
Collision-Coalescence (warm rain process)
Collisions between droplets of varying size and fall speeds coalesce to form larger drops
Ice Crystal Process
Water vapor directly on ice crystals which eventually become heavy enough to fall
Precipitation Types
The vertical distribution of temperature often determines the precipitation at the surface
Rain: Deep layer of above freezing air based at the surface
Snow: Occurs when the temperature is below freezing throughout the entire depth of the atmosphere
Ice Pellets: Require a shallow, above freezing layer aloft, & a deep, below freezing layer at the surface
Freezing Rain: Deep, above freezing layer aloft and a shallow, below freezing layer at the surface
Weather System Formation 									AI.III.C.K3e
Air Masses
A large body of air with generally uniform temperature and humidity
Area from which an air mass originates is called a source region
Classified according to temperature and moisture properties of the source region
Temperature Properties
Arctic: Extremely deep cold air mass; develops mostly in winter over arctic ice/snow
Polar: A relatively shallow cool to cold air mass which develops over high latitudes
Tropical: A warm to hot air mass which develops over low latitudes
Moisture Properties
Continental: A dry air mass which develops over land
Maritime: A moist air mass which develops over water
Types of Air Masses (Temperature + Moisture Properties)
Continental Arctic: Cold, dry
Continental Polar: Cold, dry
Continental Tropical: Hot, dry
Maritime Polar: Cool, moist
Maritime Tropical: Warm, moist
Maritime Arctic seldom, if ever, forms
As an air mass moves around the Earth, it can acquire different attributes
Fronts
A boundary or transition zone between two air masses
Most weather occurs along fronts
Classified by which type of air mass (cold or warm) is replacing the other
Fronts are usually detectable at the surface in several ways:
Significant temperature gradients
Converging winds
Pressure typically decreases as a front approaches and increases after it passes
Fronts do not only exist at the surface, but also have a vertical structure described here:
Clouds 												AI.III.C.K3f
Vertical Motion & Cloud Formation
Air cools as it rises
As pressure decreases, the air parcel expands, which requires energy, cooling the air
Reaches a point where temp and dewpoint are equal, and the particle becomes saturated
Lifted Condensation Level (LCL): Level at which a parcel of air becomes saturated
Lifting above the LCL results in condensation, cloud formation and heat release
As the air parcel expands and cools, water vapor content decreases
Some water vapor is condensed to droplets or deposited into ice crystals to form a cloud
The cloud grows vertically as the parcel continues to rise
The opposite occurs as a particle descends
Sources of Vertical Motion
Orographic Effects
Wind blowing across mountains and valleys causing the air to ascend/descend
Frictional Effects
Winds diverge away from high pressure causing air to sink, compress, & war, dissipating clouds
Winds converge into low pressure causing air to rise, expand & cool, favoring clouds & precipitation
Frontal Lift
Cold, denser air wedges under warm, less dense air, forcing it upward
Buoyancy
Air near the ground can warm at different rates
Temperature differences result in different air densities, allowing warm air to rise and cold to sink
Clouds
Cloud Forms
Cirri-form
High level clouds above 20,000’ usually composed of ice crystals
Typically, thin, and white
Occur in fair weather and point in the direction of air movement
Nimbo-form (Nimbus comes from the Latin word meaning rain)
Typically, between 7,000 and 15,000’ with steady precipitation
As clouds thicken and precipitation falls, the bases tend to lower
Cumuli-form
White, fluffy cotton balls (show the vertical motion in the atmosphere)
Flat cloud base indicates the level of condensation/cloud formation
Height depends on humidity of rising air (more humid = lower base)
Tops can reach > 60,000’
Strati-form (Stratus is Latin for layer or blanket)
Featureless low layer that can cover the entire sky, like a blanket
Usually only a few hundred feet AGL
As fog lifts due to heating, it can form a layer of low stratus clouds
Cloud Levels
High, Middle, and Low
In each level, the clouds may be divided by type
Cloud Types (next page)
High Clouds
Middle Clouds
Low Clouds
Turbulence 											AI.III.C.K3g
Caused by convective currents, obstructions in the wind flow, and wind shear
Convective Turbulence
Turbulent vertical motions resulting from convective currents and the rising and sinking of air
Billowy cumuliform clouds indicate convective turbulence
When air is too dry for cumuliform clouds, convective currents can still be active
Mechanical Turbulence
Caused by obstructions to the wind flow, such as trees, buildings, and mountains
Mountain Waves: Stable air passes over a mountain, developing waves above/downwind of mountains
Often produce violent down drafts on the immediate leeward side of the mountain barrier
Cap clouds, cirrocumulus standing lenticular, altocumulus standing lenticular & rotor clouds are signs
Wind Shear Turbulence
Wind shear is the rate of change in wind direction and/or speed per unit distance
Often occur across temperature inversion layers, which can generate turbulence
Clear Air Turbulence
A higher altitude turbulence phenomenon occurring in cloud-free regions associated with wind shear, particularly between the core of a jet stream and the surrounding air
Thunderstorms 										AI.III.C.K3h
Ingredients: Sufficient Water Vapor, Unstable Air, Lifting Mechanism
Life Cycle
Towering Cumulus: A strong convective updraft
Mature: When precipitation reaches the surface
Precipitation descends drags air downward, creating a strong downdraft alongside the updraft
Dissipating: Strong downdraft embedded within the area of precipitation
Subsiding air replaces the updraft, cutting off the moisture provided by the updraft
Types of Thunderstorms
Single Cell
Consists of only one cell. Single cell thunderstorms are rare; almost all are multicell
Multicell
Consists of a cluster of cells at various stages of their life cycle
As the first cell matures, it is carried downwind, and a new cell forms upwind to take its place
New cells continue to form as long as ingredients exist
A line of thunderstorms can extend laterally for hundreds of miles
Often too high to fly over, too long to fly around and too dangerous to fly under
Supercell
Dangerous convective storm consisting of primarily a single, quasi-steady rotating updraft
Organized internal structure produces especially dangerous weather (updrafts up to 9,000 fpm)
May persist for hours; new cells will continue to form as long as the necessary ingredients exist
Hazards
Lightning, winds/microburst, turbulence, icing, hail, rapid altimeter changes, static electricity, tornado
Microbursts
The most severe type of wind shear; downdrafts up to 6,000 fpm
Flying through a microburst (pictured)
Performance increasing headwind, performance-decreasing downdrafts, rapidly increasing tailwind
Airplane may be forced to the ground
Indications
Visual
Intense rain shaft at the surface, but virga at cloud base
Ring of blowing dust
Alerting Systems
LLWAS-NE, TDWR, and ASR-9 WSP systems installed at major airports
Many airports, especially smaller airports, have no wind shear systems
Aviation Weather Handbook (FAA-H-8083-28)
Avoiding Microbursts/Wind Shear
Never takeoff or conduct low level operations near an active thunderstorm
LLWAS (Low Level Wind Shear Alerting System)
PIREPS
If unable to avoid, follow manufacturer’s procedures
General procedures include max power, pitch aggressively for max climb (do not stall)
Frost & Icing 									AI.III.C.K3i, AI.III.C.K3k
Frost
On cool, clear nights, cool ground can cause surrounding air to drop below the dewpoint
Moisture condenses on the ground, buildings, and other objects as dew (below freezing = frost)
Dew poses no threat to aircraft, but frost poses a definite flight safety hazard
An aircraft must be thoroughly cleaned and free of frost prior to beginning a flight
Types of Icing
Rime Icing
Rough, milky, opaque ice formed by the instant freezing of small, super cooled water droplets after they strike the aircraft
Favors colder temperatures, lower liquid water content and small droplets
Clear Icing
A glossy, clear ice formed by slow freezing of large super cooled water droplets (smears as it freezes)
Exist in warmer temperatures, higher liquid water contents, and larger droplets
More hazardous than rime ice
It tends to disrupt airflow considerably more than rime icing
It is clear and more difficult to see and therefore can be difficult to recognize
It is difficult to remove since it can spread beyond the deice/anti-ice capabilities
Mixed Icing
A mixture of clear and rime ice - Poses a similar hazard to an aircraft as clear ice
Hazards of Icing
Structural icing degrades engine performance
Destroys the smooth flow of air over the wing, increasing drag and decreasing the ability to create lift
Actual weight of ice on an aircraft is insignificant when compared to the airflow disruption it causes
Freezing Level
Be alert for icing anytime the temperature approaches 0o C and visible moisture is present
When carried above the freezing level, water becomes supercooled
Supercooled water freezes on impact with an aircraft
Abundance of large, supercooled water droplets makes clear icing very rapid between 0 & -15o C
Fog & Mist 											AI.III.C.K3j
Fog
Tiny water droplets at the surface that reduce visibility to less than 5/8 statute mile
Radiation Fog
Produced over a land area when radiational cooling reduces the air temperature below its dew point
Factors: Shallow surface layer of moist air beneath a dry layer, clear skies, light surface winds
Ground fog usually burns off rapidly after sunrise. Other radiation fog generally clears before noon
Mountain/Valley Fog
Ground cools overnight and the denser, cooler mountaintop air sinks into valleys and collects there
Most common in fall and spring, and densest near sunrise when surface temperatures are lowest
Advection Fog
Moist air moves over a colder surface, cooling the air to below its dew point
Most common along coastal areas but often moves deep in continental areas.
Upslope Fog
Moist, stable air being adiabatically cooled to or below its dewpoint as it moves up sloping terrain
Wind speeds of 5-15 knots are most favorable
Common along the eastern slopes of the Rockies, and less frequent east of the Appalachians
Frontal Fog
Formation
When warm, moist air is lifted over a front, clouds, and precipitation may form
If the cold air below is near its dewpoint, evaporation may saturate the cold air and form fog
Result is a continuous zone of condensed water droplets from the ground through the clouds
Mostly associated with warm fronts but can occur with others as well.
Steam Fog
Very cold air moves across relatively warm water, moisture evaporates to produce saturation
Rising water vapor meets the cold air & recondenses, rising with air being warmed from below
Appears as rising streamers that resemble steam
Often very shallow; expect convective turbulence flying through it
Freezing Fog
Tiny, supercooled liquid water droplets in fog freeze on exposed surfaces at or below freezing
Mist
Tiny water droplets reducing visibility to less than 7 SM, but greater than, or equal to, 5/8 SM
Forms a thin grayish veil covering the landscape
Intermediate between fog and haze
Obstructions to Visibility 									AI.III.C.K3l
Haze
Numerous extremely small particles giving the air an opalescent appearance
Occurs in stable air and is usually only a few thousand feet thick, but may extend upwards of 15,000’
Visibility varies greatly depending on whether you’re facing into or away from the sun
Smoke
Suspension of small particles in the air produced by fires, industrial burning, etc.
Can reduce visibility to zero and contains many highly toxic compounds, like carbon monoxide (CO)
Must be dispersed by movement of air
Volcanic Ash
Made up of fine particles of rock powder from a volcano (ash is composed of silica (glass))
Ash may not be visible at night or in IMC, even if visible, it’s hard to distinguish from ordinary clouds
Very hazardous to aircraft
Piston aircraft: May not lose power, but severe engine damage is likely
Causes abrasive damage
Blowing Snow
Snow lifted from the surface by the wind to a height of 6’ or more; Reduces visibility to less than 7 SM
Whiteout: Strong winds keep snow suspended up to 50’, obscuring the sky and reducing visibility to zero
Visibility improves rapidly when the wind subsides
Dust Storms
Originate over regions when fine-grained soils, rich in clay and silt, are exposed to strong winds
Most common in the Southwest US
Reduce visibility to near zero
Creation & Dissipation
Extreme heating of barren ground + turbulent unstable air mass
Surface winds 15 knots or greater (35 knots over desert rock fragments)
Average height is 3,000 to 6,000’, but can reach up to 15,000’
Strong cooling after sunset settles the dust (temperature inversion)
Hazards
Visibility can drop to zero in a matter of seconds
Dust can clog intakes, damage systems, and affect human health
Slant range visibility is greatly reduced compared to report surface visibility
Sandstorms
Particles of sand carried aloft by a strong wind
Like dust storms but on a more localized level since the sand particles are heavier (10’ to 50’ AGL)
Haboob
Dust storm that forms as cold downdrafts from a thunderstorm lift dust and sand into the air
Often short lived, but can be intense

METAR, TAF, & GFA
METAR (Aviation Routine Weather Report)
An observation of current surface weather reported in a standard international format
Terminal Aerodrome Forecast (TAF)
A terminal aerodrome forecast is a report established for the 5 sm radius around an airport
Valid for a 24-hour period, updated four times a day at 0000Z, 0600Z, 1200Z, and 1800Z.
Graphical Forecasts for Aviation (GFA) – replaced the Area Forecast (FA)

Note: Not required by the ACS, but if used during the checkride, the examiner may ask about it

Takes weather models and applies statistics/historical observations to produce a specific forecast

Overview
Depicts areas forecast to have severe and non-severe (general) convection over 8 days

RM: In-Flight Weather Advisories 						AI.III.C.K2g, AI.III.C.R1c
Forecasts detailing potentially hazardous weather
AIRMET (WA)
Information of interest to all, but the weather section is specifically dangerous to light aircraft
Issued every 6 hours with intermediate updates as needed
3 Types
SIERRA: Denotes IFR and mountain obscurement
TANGO: Denotes turbulence, strong surface winds, and low-level wind shear
ZULU: Denotes icing and freezing levels
SIGMET (WS)
In flight advisory concerning non-convective weather that is potentially hazardous to all aircraft
Severe icing; extreme turbulence; Clear Air Turbulence (CAT); dust/sandstorms; volcanic ash
Unscheduled forecasts valid for 4 hours (hurricane SIGMET is valid for 6 hours)
Convective SIGMENT (WST)
Weather advisory issued for hazardous convective weather that affects the safety of every flight
Issued for: Embedded thunderstorms, line of thunderstorms, as well as:
Severe Thunderstorms with
Surface winds greater than 50 knots
Hail at the surface ≥ ¾ inch in diameter
Tornadoes
Thunderstorms with heavy or greater precip affecting 40% or more of a 3,000 ft2 or greater area
Center Weather Advisory (CWA)
Unscheduled inflight, flow control, air traffic, and air crew advisory
Produced for weather beginning in the next 2 hours, and will be issued:
As a supplement to existing SIGMENT, Convective SIGMENT or AIRMET
When an inflight advisory has not been issued but weather conditions meet SIGMET/AIRMET criteria based on pilot reports & reinforced by other meteorological conditions
When observed or developing weather does not meet SIGMET, Convective SIGMET, or AIRMET criteria but pilot reports indicate the weather will adversely affect safe flow of air traffic
Inflight Weather Advisory Broadcasts
ARTCCs broadcast Convective SIGMET, SIGMENT, or CWAs once on all frequencies (not emergency) when any part of the area described is within 150 miles of their airspace
PIREPS
Pilot generated report concerning meteorological phenomena encountered in flight
Required Elements: Type, location, time, altitude, aircraft type, and at least 1 describing element
Urgent PIREP (UUA): Issued for tornados, severe/extreme turbulence, severe icing, hail, LLWS within 2,000’ of the surface, volcanic ash, or any other phenomena considered to be hazardous
Route PIRPER (UA): Issued based on pilot reports that do not contain urgent information

OVERVIEW

WHAT
First, a discussion of weather – how it forms, interacts, and its relation to flying. And second, through a complex system of weather services, government agencies, and independent weather observers, pilots are given vast information regarding weather patterns, trends, and characteristics in the form of up-to-date weather reports and forecasts.

WHY
This knowledge, and the reports and forecasts enable pilots to make informed decisions regarding weather and flight safety.
Cold Front
Warm Front

Cold fronts have a steep slope, and the warm air is forced up abruptly.
If the warm rising air is unstable, this often leads to a narrow band of showers and thunderstorms along, or just ahead of, the front.

Warm fronts have a gentle slope, so the warm air rising along the frontal surface is gradual.
This favors the development of widespread layered or stratiform cloudiness and precipitation along, and ahead of, the front if the warm rising air is stable.
Stationary Front
Occluded Front
Stationary frontal slopes can vary, but clouds and precipitation would still form in the warm rising air along the front.

Cold fronts typically move faster than warm fronts, so in time they catch up to warm fronts. As the two fronts merge, an occluded front forms.
The cold air undercuts the retreating cooler air mass associated with the warm front, further lifting the already rising warm air
Clouds and precipitation can occur in the areas of frontal lift along, ahead of, and behind the surface position of an occluded front
Cirrus
Cirrocumulus
Cirrostratus

Detached cirriform elements in the form of white, delicate filaments of white patches, or narrow bands. 

Many of the ice crystal particles are sufficiently large to acquire appreciable speed of fall; therefore, the clouds often trail downward in well-defined wisps called mares’ tails. 

Cirrus clouds in themselves have little effect on aircraft and contain no significant icing or turbulence.

A cirriform type appearing as a thin, patch, sheet, or layer of  white could without shading, and is composed of very small elements in the form of grains, ripples, etc. 

May be composed of highly super cooled water droplets, as well as small ice crystals, or a mix of both. 

Pilots can expect some turbulence and icing

Appears as a whiteish veil, usually fibrous but sometimes smooth, that may totally cover the sky, and that often produces halo phenomena. 

May be so thin and transparent as to render it nearly indiscernible – the existence of a halo around the sun or moon may be the only revealing feature. 

Composed primarily of ice crystals and contain little, if any, icing and no turbulence.
Altocumulus
Altocumulus Lenticularis
Altostratus

White and/or grey in color, that occurs as a layer or patch with a wave aspect, the elements of which appear as laminae, rounded masses, rolls, etc. 

Small liquid water droplets compose the major part of the composition of altocumulus. This results in a sharp outline and small internal visibility. At very low temperatures ice crystals may form. 

Expect some turbulence and small amounts of icing

Commonly known as Altocumulus Standing Lenticular, they are an orographic cloud. 

Often form in patches in the shape of almonds or wave clouds. These formations are caused by wave motions in the atmosphere and are frequently seen in mountainous or hilly areas. The cloud is usually stationary or slow moving.

The clouds do not necessarily give an indication of the intensity of turbulence or strength of updrafts and downdrafts.

A gray or bluish sheet or layer of striated, fibrous, or uniform appearance. 

It often totally covers the sky. Portions of the layer are thin, and it can have irregularly shaped and spaced gaps and rifts.

Layers in the cloud:
Upper - mostly ice crystals
Middle - mixed ice crystals and/or snowflakes and super cooled water droplets
Lower- mostly super cooled or ordinary water droplets

Expect little to no turbulence, but light to moderate icing in the super cooled water.
Nimbostratus
Nimbostratus
Nimbostratus

A gray cloud layer, often dark, rendered diffuse by continuously falling rain, snow, ice pellets, etc., which, in most cases, reaches the ground. Not accompanied by lightning, thunder, or hail. 

Composed of suspended water droplets, sometimes super cooled, and failing raindrops/snow crystals or snowflakes. Has no well-defined base. A false base may occur where snow melts into rain. 

It produces very little turbulence but can pose a serious icing problem if temperatures are near or below freezing.

A gray cloud layer, often dark, rendered diffuse by continuously falling rain, snow, ice pellets, etc., which, in most cases, reaches the ground. Not accompanied by lightning, thunder, or hail. 

Composed of suspended water droplets, sometimes super cooled, and failing raindrops/snow crystals or snowflakes. Has no well-defined base. A false base may occur where snow melts into rain. 

It produces very little turbulence but can pose a serious icing problem if temperatures are near or below freezing.
Cumulus & Towering Cumulus
Stratocumulus
Stratus

Individual detached elements that are generally dense. They develop vertically, appearing as rising mounds, the upper parts of which often resemble cauliflower. Sunlit parts are white, while their bases are darker and nearly horizontal.  The first stage of a thunderstorm.

If rain occurs, it is usually showery.  

For cumulus with little vertical development, expect some turbulence but no significant icing. For towering cumulus, expect very strong turbulence and clear icing above the freezing level.

Predominantly stratiform, in the form of a gray/whiteish layer or patch which nearly always has dark parts and is non-fibrous. Rounded/roll-shaped and usually are in orderly groups.

Composed of small water droplets, and sometimes larger droplets, soft hail, even snowflakes. The highest liquid content is in the tops (icing potential). Virga may form under the cloud. Precipitation rarely occurs. 

Expect some turbulence and possible icing. Ceiling & vis are usually better with low stratus.

A cloud type in the form of a gray layer with a fairly uniform base. The composition is quite uniform, usually of fairly widely dispersed water droplets, and at lower temperatures, ice crystals (rare).

III.C. Weather Information
Introduction
How
Atmospheric Composition & Stability 							AI.III.C.K3a
4 gases make up 99.998% of the atmosphere
Nitrogen, Oxygen, Argon, and Carbon Dioxide
The Atmosphere is divided into 5 concentric layers
Troposphere
Surface up to about 36,000’ high (varies with temperature variations)
Temperature decreases with height & almost all weather occurs in this region
Transition layer between the troposphere and they layer above is called the tropopause
Stratosphere
Tropopause up to 31 miles high (Holds 19% of the atmosphere’s gases, but little water)
Temperature increases with height due to the absorption of UV radiation
Commercial aircraft often cruise in the lower stratosphere to avoid turbulence/convection
Mesosphere
Stratopause to about 53 miles above the Earth.
Gases continue to thin leading to a decrease in temperature with height
Thermosphere
Mesopause to 430 miles above the Earth (known as the upper atmosphere)
Temp increases with height and can reach 2,000 degrees Celsius near the top of the layer
High energy UV and X-ray radiation from the sun is absorbed
Exosphere
Thermopause to 6,200 miles above the surface (outermost layer of the atmosphere)
Atoms and molecules escape into space, and where satellites orbit the Earth
Standard Atmosphere
59o F / 15o C &  29.92” Hg
Average of conditions throughout the atmosphere for all latitudes, seasons, and altitudes
Wind 												AI.III.C.K3b
Air in motion relative to the surface. Wind causes the formation, dissipation, and redistribution of weather
Forces that Affect the Wind
Pressure Gradient Force (PGF)
Wind flows from areas of high to low pressure. These different pressures create the PGF
When a pressure difference develops, the PGF makes the wind blow to equalize the differences
Wind speed is proportional to PGF which is proportional to the contour/isobar gradient
Coriolis Force (pictured, right)
Deflects air to the right in the Northern Hemisphere & left in the Southern Hemisphere
At a right angle to wind direction
Directly proportional to wind speed
If wind speed doubles, Coriolis doubles
Coriolis varies with latitude
Zero at the equator & maximum at each pole
Friction
Friction between wind and the surface slows the wind
Rougher terrain and stronger winds = greater friction
Insignificant above the lowest few thousand feet or so
Above the friction layer, only the PGF and Coriolis force affect the horizontal motion of the air
Adverse Winds
Wind Shear
What is it?
A sudden, drastic change in wind speed and/or direction over a very small area
Can occur at any altitude
Low-level wind shear is especially hazardous due to the proximity to the ground
Low-level wind shear is commonly associated with passing frontal systems, thunderstorms, temperature inversions, and strong upper-level winds (> 25 knots)
Why is it dangerous?
Can cause violent updrafts/downdrafts, and abrupt changes to horizontal movement
It can rapidly change performance and disrupt the normal flight attitude, for example:
A tailwind can quickly change to a headwind, increasing airspeed and performance
A headwind can quickly change to a tailwind, decreasing airspeed and performance
Although reported, it often remains undetected
Be alert for wind shear, especially when flying around thunderstorms & frontal systems
Mountain Waves (AIM 7-6-7j)
What is it?
The atmosphere is a fluid in motion
Just as a stream develops waves & eddies as it passes obstructions, so does the atmosphere
When the atmosphere encounters a mountainous barrier, and the wind is sufficiently strong and the atmosphere is stable, a wave will develop
Air hits the upwind side, creating a smooth updraft
Passing the crest, it becomes a turbulent downdraft
Turns into a wave that can last for miles
Hazards
Strong down drafts and/or turbulence on the immediate leeward side of the mountain
Visual Indicators
Sharp-edged, lens-shaped lenticular clouds
With sufficient moisture, clouds can include:
Cap clouds, Cirrocumulus Standing Lenticular (CCSL), Altocumulus Standing Lenticular (ACSL), and rotor clouds
These clouds provide evidence of mountain waves, but may be absent if the air is too dry
Types of Waves
For significantly more info, Aviation Weather Handbook Ch. 16 discusses many wave types
Gravity Waves, Kelvin-Helmholtz (K-H) Waves, Vertically Propagating Mountain Waves, Trapped Lee Waves, and more
Temperature											AI.III.C.K3c
Represents the average kinetic energy of the molecules in matte
Heat Transfer
Heat transfer is a transfer of energy due to temperature difference
The heat source for the planet is the sun. Energy from the sun is transferred to the Earth’s surface. There are 3 ways heat is transferred into and through our atmosphere:
Radiation: Ex. Being near a fireplace, the sun radiating heat to the earth
Conduction: Transfer of energy from one substance to another
Convection: Transport of heat within a fluid, such as air or water
Because air is a poor thermal conductor, convection plays a vital role in the Earth’s atmospheric heat transfer process
Temperature & the Earth/Atmosphere
Thermal Response: Water is much more resistant to temperature changes than land
Temperature Variations with Altitude
Temperature generally decreases at an average of 2o Celsius per 1,000’
But in the troposphere, temperature can remain constant or increase with altitude changes
Isothermal Layer: An atmospheric layer where temperature remains constant with height
Temperature Inversion: A layer in which the temperature increases with altitude
Moisture & Precipitation 									AI.III.C.K3d
Ingredients for Precipitation
Water Vapor
Sufficient Lifting - condenses the water vapor into clouds
Growth Process - allows cold droplets to grow large and heavy enough to fall as precipitation
Two growth processes allow cloud droplets to grow large enough to fall as precipitation
Collision-Coalescence (warm rain process)
Collisions between droplets of varying size and fall speeds coalesce to form larger drops
Ice Crystal Process
Water vapor directly on ice crystals which eventually become heavy enough to fall
Precipitation Types
The vertical distribution of temperature often determines the precipitation at the surface
Rain: Deep layer of above freezing air based at the surface
Snow: Occurs when the temperature is below freezing throughout the entire depth of the atmosphere
Ice Pellets: Require a shallow, above freezing layer aloft, & a deep, below freezing layer at the surface
Freezing Rain: Deep, above freezing layer aloft and a shallow, below freezing layer at the surface
Weather System Formation 									AI.III.C.K3e
Air Masses
A large body of air with generally uniform temperature and humidity
Area from which an air mass originates is called a source region
Classified according to temperature and moisture properties of the source region
Temperature Properties
Arctic: Extremely deep cold air mass; develops mostly in winter over arctic ice/snow
Polar: A relatively shallow cool to cold air mass which develops over high latitudes
Tropical: A warm to hot air mass which develops over low latitudes
Moisture Properties
Continental: A dry air mass which develops over land
Maritime: A moist air mass which develops over water
Types of Air Masses (Temperature + Moisture Properties)
Continental Arctic: Cold, dry
Continental Polar: Cold, dry
Continental Tropical: Hot, dry
Maritime Polar: Cool, moist
Maritime Tropical: Warm, moist
Maritime Arctic seldom, if ever, forms
As an air mass moves around the Earth, it can acquire different attributes
Fronts
A boundary or transition zone between two air masses
Most weather occurs along fronts
Classified by which type of air mass (cold or warm) is replacing the other
Fronts are usually detectable at the surface in several ways:
Significant temperature gradients
Converging winds
Pressure typically decreases as a front approaches and increases after it passes
Fronts do not only exist at the surface, but also have a vertical structure described here:
Clouds 												AI.III.C.K3f
Vertical Motion & Cloud Formation
Air cools as it rises
As pressure decreases, the air parcel expands, which requires energy, cooling the air
Reaches a point where temp and dewpoint are equal, and the particle becomes saturated
Lifted Condensation Level (LCL): Level at which a parcel of air becomes saturated
Lifting above the LCL results in condensation, cloud formation and heat release
As the air parcel expands and cools, water vapor content decreases
Some water vapor is condensed to droplets or deposited into ice crystals to form a cloud
The cloud grows vertically as the parcel continues to rise
The opposite occurs as a particle descends
Sources of Vertical Motion
Orographic Effects
Wind blowing across mountains and valleys causing the air to ascend/descend
Frictional Effects
Winds diverge away from high pressure causing air to sink, compress, & war, dissipating clouds
Winds converge into low pressure causing air to rise, expand & cool, favoring clouds & precipitation
Frontal Lift
Cold, denser air wedges under warm, less dense air, forcing it upward
Buoyancy
Air near the ground can warm at different rates
Temperature differences result in different air densities, allowing warm air to rise and cold to sink
Clouds
Cloud Forms
Cirri-form
High level clouds above 20,000’ usually composed of ice crystals
Typically, thin, and white
Occur in fair weather and point in the direction of air movement
Nimbo-form (Nimbus comes from the Latin word meaning rain)
Typically, between 7,000 and 15,000’ with steady precipitation
As clouds thicken and precipitation falls, the bases tend to lower
Cumuli-form
White, fluffy cotton balls (show the vertical motion in the atmosphere)
Flat cloud base indicates the level of condensation/cloud formation
Height depends on humidity of rising air (more humid = lower base)
Tops can reach > 60,000’
Strati-form (Stratus is Latin for layer or blanket)
Featureless low layer that can cover the entire sky, like a blanket
Usually only a few hundred feet AGL
As fog lifts due to heating, it can form a layer of low stratus clouds
Cloud Levels
High, Middle, and Low
In each level, the clouds may be divided by type
Cloud Types (next page)
High Clouds
Middle Clouds
Low Clouds
Turbulence 											AI.III.C.K3g
Caused by convective currents, obstructions in the wind flow, and wind shear
Convective Turbulence
Turbulent vertical motions resulting from convective currents and the rising and sinking of air
Billowy cumuliform clouds indicate convective turbulence
When air is too dry for cumuliform clouds, convective currents can still be active
Mechanical Turbulence
Caused by obstructions to the wind flow, such as trees, buildings, and mountains
Mountain Waves: Stable air passes over a mountain, developing waves above/downwind of mountains
Often produce violent down drafts on the immediate leeward side of the mountain barrier
Cap clouds, cirrocumulus standing lenticular, altocumulus standing lenticular & rotor clouds are signs
Wind Shear Turbulence
Wind shear is the rate of change in wind direction and/or speed per unit distance
Often occur across temperature inversion layers, which can generate turbulence
Clear Air Turbulence
A higher altitude turbulence phenomenon occurring in cloud-free regions associated with wind shear, particularly between the core of a jet stream and the surrounding air
Thunderstorms 										AI.III.C.K3h
Ingredients: Sufficient Water Vapor, Unstable Air, Lifting Mechanism
Life Cycle
Towering Cumulus: A strong convective updraft
Mature: When precipitation reaches the surface
Precipitation descends drags air downward, creating a strong downdraft alongside the updraft
Dissipating: Strong downdraft embedded within the area of precipitation
Subsiding air replaces the updraft, cutting off the moisture provided by the updraft
Types of Thunderstorms
Single Cell
Consists of only one cell. Single cell thunderstorms are rare; almost all are multicell
Multicell
Consists of a cluster of cells at various stages of their life cycle
As the first cell matures, it is carried downwind, and a new cell forms upwind to take its place
New cells continue to form as long as ingredients exist
A line of thunderstorms can extend laterally for hundreds of miles
Often too high to fly over, too long to fly around and too dangerous to fly under
Supercell
Dangerous convective storm consisting of primarily a single, quasi-steady rotating updraft
Organized internal structure produces especially dangerous weather (updrafts up to 9,000 fpm)
May persist for hours; new cells will continue to form as long as the necessary ingredients exist
Hazards
Lightning, winds/microburst, turbulence, icing, hail, rapid altimeter changes, static electricity, tornado
Microbursts
The most severe type of wind shear; downdrafts up to 6,000 fpm
Flying through a microburst (pictured)
Performance increasing headwind, performance-decreasing downdrafts, rapidly increasing tailwind
Airplane may be forced to the ground
Indications
Visual
Intense rain shaft at the surface, but virga at cloud base
Ring of blowing dust
Alerting Systems
LLWAS-NE, TDWR, and ASR-9 WSP systems installed at major airports
Many airports, especially smaller airports, have no wind shear systems
Aviation Weather Handbook (FAA-H-8083-28)
Avoiding Microbursts/Wind Shear
Never takeoff or conduct low level operations near an active thunderstorm
LLWAS (Low Level Wind Shear Alerting System)
PIREPS
If unable to avoid, follow manufacturer’s procedures
General procedures include max power, pitch aggressively for max climb (do not stall)
Frost & Icing 									AI.III.C.K3i, AI.III.C.K3k
Frost
On cool, clear nights, cool ground can cause surrounding air to drop below the dewpoint
Moisture condenses on the ground, buildings, and other objects as dew (below freezing = frost)
Dew poses no threat to aircraft, but frost poses a definite flight safety hazard
An aircraft must be thoroughly cleaned and free of frost prior to beginning a flight
Types of Icing
Rime Icing
Rough, milky, opaque ice formed by the instant freezing of small, super cooled water droplets after they strike the aircraft
Favors colder temperatures, lower liquid water content and small droplets
Clear Icing
A glossy, clear ice formed by slow freezing of large super cooled water droplets (smears as it freezes)
Exist in warmer temperatures, higher liquid water contents, and larger droplets
More hazardous than rime ice
It tends to disrupt airflow considerably more than rime icing
It is clear and more difficult to see and therefore can be difficult to recognize
It is difficult to remove since it can spread beyond the deice/anti-ice capabilities
Mixed Icing
A mixture of clear and rime ice - Poses a similar hazard to an aircraft as clear ice
Hazards of Icing
Structural icing degrades engine performance
Destroys the smooth flow of air over the wing, increasing drag and decreasing the ability to create lift
Actual weight of ice on an aircraft is insignificant when compared to the airflow disruption it causes
Freezing Level
Be alert for icing anytime the temperature approaches 0o C and visible moisture is present
When carried above the freezing level, water becomes supercooled
Supercooled water freezes on impact with an aircraft
Abundance of large, supercooled water droplets makes clear icing very rapid between 0 & -15o C
Fog & Mist 											AI.III.C.K3j
Fog
Tiny water droplets at the surface that reduce visibility to less than 5/8 statute mile
Radiation Fog
Produced over a land area when radiational cooling reduces the air temperature below its dew point
Factors: Shallow surface layer of moist air beneath a dry layer, clear skies, light surface winds
Ground fog usually burns off rapidly after sunrise. Other radiation fog generally clears before noon
Mountain/Valley Fog
Ground cools overnight and the denser, cooler mountaintop air sinks into valleys and collects there
Most common in fall and spring, and densest near sunrise when surface temperatures are lowest
Advection Fog
Moist air moves over a colder surface, cooling the air to below its dew point
Most common along coastal areas but often moves deep in continental areas.
Upslope Fog
Moist, stable air being adiabatically cooled to or below its dewpoint as it moves up sloping terrain
Wind speeds of 5-15 knots are most favorable
Common along the eastern slopes of the Rockies, and less frequent east of the Appalachians
Frontal Fog
Formation
When warm, moist air is lifted over a front, clouds, and precipitation may form
If the cold air below is near its dewpoint, evaporation may saturate the cold air and form fog
Result is a continuous zone of condensed water droplets from the ground through the clouds
Mostly associated with warm fronts but can occur with others as well.
Steam Fog
Very cold air moves across relatively warm water, moisture evaporates to produce saturation
Rising water vapor meets the cold air & recondenses, rising with air being warmed from below
Appears as rising streamers that resemble steam
Often very shallow; expect convective turbulence flying through it
Freezing Fog
Tiny, supercooled liquid water droplets in fog freeze on exposed surfaces at or below freezing
Mist
Tiny water droplets reducing visibility to less than 7 SM, but greater than, or equal to, 5/8 SM
Forms a thin grayish veil covering the landscape
Intermediate between fog and haze
Obstructions to Visibility 									AI.III.C.K3l
Haze
Numerous extremely small particles giving the air an opalescent appearance
Occurs in stable air and is usually only a few thousand feet thick, but may extend upwards of 15,000’
Visibility varies greatly depending on whether you’re facing into or away from the sun
Smoke
Suspension of small particles in the air produced by fires, industrial burning, etc.
Can reduce visibility to zero and contains many highly toxic compounds, like carbon monoxide (CO)
Must be dispersed by movement of air
Volcanic Ash
Made up of fine particles of rock powder from a volcano (ash is composed of silica (glass))
Ash may not be visible at night or in IMC, even if visible, it’s hard to distinguish from ordinary clouds
Very hazardous to aircraft
Piston aircraft: May not lose power, but severe engine damage is likely
Causes abrasive damage
Blowing Snow
Snow lifted from the surface by the wind to a height of 6’ or more; Reduces visibility to less than 7 SM
Whiteout: Strong winds keep snow suspended up to 50’, obscuring the sky and reducing visibility to zero
Visibility improves rapidly when the wind subsides
Dust Storms
Originate over regions when fine-grained soils, rich in clay and silt, are exposed to strong winds
Most common in the Southwest US
Reduce visibility to near zero
Creation & Dissipation
Extreme heating of barren ground + turbulent unstable air mass
Surface winds 15 knots or greater (35 knots over desert rock fragments)
Average height is 3,000 to 6,000’, but can reach up to 15,000’
Strong cooling after sunset settles the dust (temperature inversion)
Hazards
Visibility can drop to zero in a matter of seconds
Dust can clog intakes, damage systems, and affect human health
Slant range visibility is greatly reduced compared to report surface visibility
Sandstorms
Particles of sand carried aloft by a strong wind
Like dust storms but on a more localized level since the sand particles are heavier (10’ to 50’ AGL)
Haboob
Dust storm that forms as cold downdrafts from a thunderstorm lift dust and sand into the air
Often short lived, but can be intense
Weather Briefings & Information								AI.III.C.K1
General awareness of the overall weather: Internet, Weather Apps, TV, etc.
Used in the weeks/days leading up to the flight (big picture awareness)
Detailed Weather Briefing (Specific to the flight)
Importance of a Thorough Weather Briefing
FAR 91.103 – As PIC, you are required to become familiar with the weather reports and forecasts
Know what to expect and alerts the pilot to changing/unexpected conditions en route
Immensely important in making an educated Go/No Go Decision

FSS (1-800-WX BRIEF or 1800wxbrief.com)
NWS – National Weather Service - Aviationweather.gov
ForeFlight - Briefings are timestamped and stored to comply with FAR 91.103
AIM 7-1-2-C: Pilots can receive a regulatory compliant briefing without contacting flight service
AC 91-92 – Pilot’s Guide to a Preflight Briefing
RM: Inflight Weather Sources
FSS Frequencies - as published, or 122.2
ForeFlight, or other apps (with data connection)
Satellite Weather - Current weather available to appropriately equipped aircraft
FIS-B (Flight Information Service Broadcast – Part of the ADS-B system)
Weather Reports and Charts 					AI.III.C.K2a, AI.III.C.K2c, AI.III.C.K2d
METAR, TAF, & GFA
METAR (Aviation Routine Weather Report)
An observation of current surface weather reported in a standard international format
Terminal Aerodrome Forecast (TAF)
A terminal aerodrome forecast is a report established for the 5 sm radius around an airport
Valid for a 24-hour period, updated four times a day at 0000Z, 0600Z, 1200Z, and 1800Z.
Graphical Forecasts for Aviation (GFA) – replaced the Area Forecast (FA)
GFA Tool – Aviationweather.gov/gfa
Complete picture of the weather for US, Gulf, Caribbean and portions of the Atlantic/Pacific
Observational data, forecasts, warnings, T-storms, clouds, precip, icing, turbulence, wind, more
Tools
GFA User’s Guide - Weather.gov
GFA Tutorial Video – Youtube.com
Product Description Doc – National Weather Service
Model Output Statistics (MOS)
Note: Not required by the ACS, but if used during the checkride, the examiner may ask about it
What is it?
Takes weather models and applies statistics/historical observations to produce a specific forecast
Completely automated
Temp, chance and type of precipitation/thunderstorms, cloud cover and height, wind speed and direction at specific points across the country
Uses: Better weather picture for aviation planning purposes
Limitations
Not a legal weather source
Cannot forecast
Multiple cloud layers, Forecast showers or fog in the vicinity, Precipitation intensity, Non-convective LLWS, No significant weather, Variable winds
Precipitation discrimination
Currently only in the US
Where to find it
ForeFlight – Airport weather tab
NWS MOS Text Bulletins
Raw MOS data breakdown: JetStream Max: MOS
Surface Analysis Chart 									AI.III.C.K2b
Depicts surface weather covering contiguous 48 states
Pressure, fronts, temps, dewpoints, wind direction/speed, local weather, visual obstructions
Computer prepared report transmitted every 3 hours covering contiguous 48 states/adjacent areas
Chart Symbols
Additional chart symbols & explanations in the PowerPoint & detailed CFI lessons
Surface weather observations for reporting points across the US can be depicted
Each reporting point is illustrated by a station model (NWS Plot Model is pictured top right, NWS aviation model pictured bottom right). A station model will include:
Type of Observation, Sky Cover, Clouds, Sea Level Pressure (SLP), Pressure Change/Tendency, Precipitation, Dewpoint, Present Weather, Temperature, Wind
Example Charts
Left: Surface analysis with surface observations, Center: Surface analysis with radar composite, Right: Surface analysis with satellite composite
NOAA Weather Prediction Center Surface Analysis Chart
Ceiling & Visibility Chart (CVA) 								AI.III.C.K2b
https://aviationweather.gov/gfa/#cigvis
Use the Ceiling, Visibility, or Flight Category drop down for a large-scale overview of ceiling/vis info
Drop down at top right (icon depicted to the right)
Use the legend icon at the bottom right to view color meanings
Combines satellite & surface observations to show ceiling & visibility across the US
Used for big picture planning and to avoid hazardous ceiling and visibility conditions
Winds & Temperatures Aloft Chart (FB) – AWS Winds/Temps				AI.III.C.K2e
Provide wind and temperature forecasts for specific locations four times a day
Wind
Direction = true north; Speed = knots (No forecasts within 1,500’ of station elevation)
First 2 numbers are direction; Second 2 are speed
Temperature (Celsius)
No forecasts within 2,500 feet of station elevation
Temperatures above 24,000 feet MSL are always negative
FB are outdated and archaic relative to the NWS’ Rapid Refresh model that updates every hour
Convective Outlook Chart									AI.III.C.K2f
Overview
Depicts areas forecast to have severe and non-severe (general) convection over 8 days
4 charts: Day 1, Day 2, Day 3, Days 4-8
Aviation Weather Convective Outlook Chart
5 Levels of Risk (Day 1-3 Charts)
5 levels of risk + thunderstorm coverage & intensity of severe weather
General (TSTM)
Marginal (MRGL), Slight (SLGT), Enhanced (ENH), Moderate (MDT), High (HIGH)
Days 1 & 2: Also contain individual severe probabilities for tornados, wind, and/or hail
Day 3: Combined probability of all 3 types of severe weather
Graphic Probability Requirements (probabilities are within 25 miles of any point)
Day 4-8 Chart
Two thresholds of 15% and 30% can be forecast (equivalent to slight and enhanced)
If no 15% areas forecast, you’ll see Predictability too low, or Potential too low
RM: In-Flight Weather Advisories 						AI.III.C.K2g, AI.III.C.R1c
Forecasts detailing potentially hazardous weather
AIRMET (WA)
Information of interest to all, but the weather section is specifically dangerous to light aircraft
Issued every 6 hours with intermediate updates as needed
3 Types
SIERRA: Denotes IFR and mountain obscurement
TANGO: Denotes turbulence, strong surface winds, and low-level wind shear
ZULU: Denotes icing and freezing levels
SIGMET (WS)
In flight advisory concerning non-convective weather that is potentially hazardous to all aircraft
Severe icing; extreme turbulence; Clear Air Turbulence (CAT); dust/sandstorms; volcanic ash
Unscheduled forecasts valid for 4 hours (hurricane SIGMET is valid for 6 hours)
Convective SIGMENT (WST)
Weather advisory issued for hazardous convective weather that affects the safety of every flight
Issued for: Embedded thunderstorms, line of thunderstorms, as well as:
Severe Thunderstorms with
Surface winds greater than 50 knots
Hail at the surface ≥ ¾ inch in diameter
Tornadoes
Thunderstorms with heavy or greater precip affecting 40% or more of a 3,000 ft2 or greater area
Center Weather Advisory (CWA)
Unscheduled inflight, flow control, air traffic, and air crew advisory
Produced for weather beginning in the next 2 hours, and will be issued:
As a supplement to existing SIGMENT, Convective SIGMENT or AIRMET
When an inflight advisory has not been issued but weather conditions meet SIGMET/AIRMET criteria based on pilot reports & reinforced by other meteorological conditions
When observed or developing weather does not meet SIGMET, Convective SIGMET, or AIRMET criteria but pilot reports indicate the weather will adversely affect safe flow of air traffic
Inflight Weather Advisory Broadcasts
ARTCCs broadcast Convective SIGMET, SIGMENT, or CWAs once on all frequencies (not emergency) when any part of the area described is within 150 miles of their airspace
PIREPS
Pilot generated report concerning meteorological phenomena encountered in flight
Required Elements: Type, location, time, altitude, aircraft type, and at least 1 describing element
Urgent PIREP (UUA): Issued for tornados, severe/extreme turbulence, severe icing, hail, LLWS within 2,000’ of the surface, volcanic ash, or any other phenomena considered to be hazardous
Route PIRPER (UA): Issued based on pilot reports that do not contain urgent information
Other Inflight Weather Information
Contact the nearest FSS to obtain an update to a previous briefing by radio
Enroute advisories tailored to the phase of flight are available on request
RM: Onboard Weather Equipment 						AI.III.C.K4, AI.III.C.R2a
Understand the operation and limitations of any onboard equipment
ADS-B (Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast)
Free weather information on receivers that can receive the data
FIS-B (Flight Information Services-Broadcast)
Free weather information on receivers that can receive the data
Wide range of weather products with national & regional focus
Satellite weather
RM: Go/No Go Decision 									AI.III.C.R1
Consider weather factors, aircraft, and equipment to be used, as well as yourself (PAVE checklist)
Set personal weather minimums and don’t bend them 			AI.III.C.R1b, AI.III.C.R1c
Recent Experience
Ensure currency AND proficiency; don’t go beyond your abilities or the aircraft’s abilities
Recognizing Weather Hazards
Interpretation of aviation weather charts, reports, etc.
Preflight planning alerts the pilot to potential hazards
Enroute updates and inflight reports alerts the pilot to changing conditions
PIREPs, SIGMETs, METARs, LLWAS, ATC information/advice, weather tools (satellite, FIS-B), etc.
Visual indications: Cloud formations, vertical development, strong wind, etc.
Continual process of decision making 							AI.III.C.R1a
Don’t be afraid to discontinue the flight or divert, if necessary
Reduced visibility (temp/dewpoint), hazardous weather (storms, icing, turbulence, etc.), PIREPs, conditions dropping below your personal minimums, etc. may lead to the decision to divert
RM: Use & limitations of aviation weather reports and forecasts 			AI.III.C.R2b
The lesson as a whole is a discussion of these concepts
Conclusion: Brief review of the main points
